title: No prying
hook: nothing is more wretched than going round prying into others' souls (Meditations 2.13)

segments.voice: Yesterday: how fast things vanish, bodies and then their memory. Your line was so quickly. What ordinary thing did you look at and enjoy? Day five hundred thirty-seven.

It's eleven at night, and you're four years deep into the vacation photos of someone you don't even like. Or you're piecing together, from a coworker's tone and a calendar invite, exactly what's going on between those two. Nobody asked you to. It's not useful. It doesn't even feel good. And yet it's oddly hard to stop. Marcus knew the pull. A few days ago he said to watch your own mind. Today he goes further, and he doesn't soften it. No prying.
screen: `FOUR YEARS INTO SOMEONE'S PHOTOS.` → `NOBODY ASKED YOU TO.` → `NO PRYING.`

segments.voice: First, the strong word. Nothing is more wretched, Marcus says, than a person who goes round and round everything, digging into the things beneath the earth, as the poet says, and trying to guess what's in the minds of the people around them. Wretched is a big word. He means it. The prying mind is busy, restless and never full. Second, the poet. The phrase about the things beneath the earth comes from the Greek poet Pindar. Plato once borrowed it to describe a philosopher whose mind ranges over everything. Marcus turns it around: that endless searching, pointed at other people's business, is a misery, not a virtue. Third, what's enough. Instead, he says, it's enough to attend to the guiding spirit within you, and to serve it sincerely. Keep it clean of turmoil, of carelessness, and of resentment toward gods and people. You have one inner life to look after. That's a full-time job. Fourth, how to see others. And when you do look at other people, Marcus says, look with affection, because they're your kin. Sometimes, even, with a kind of pity, when they don't know good from bad, which he calls a blindness no smaller than not telling black from white. Notice the order. Not suspicion, not curiosity, not judgment. Affection first. Pity, when it's called for. Prying has no place in that list. Not my business isn't coldness. It's a way of giving people the privacy you'd want, and giving yourself back the evening.
screen: `NOTHING MORE WRETCHED THAN PRYING.` · `PINDAR'S LINE, TURNED AROUND.` · `TEND THE SPIRIT WITHIN.` · `SEE OTHERS WITH AFFECTION.` · then, large: `NOT MY BUSINESS.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Think of one place your curiosity tends to go where it isn't needed. A profile you check. A rumor you follow. A relationship you keep analyzing. Picture the pull of it. Now picture closing that door, gently, and turning back toward your own inner room. What needs tending in there today? Then think of the person you were prying into, and send them one plain thought of goodwill instead. The bell holds the time.
No prying. Marcus says nothing is more wretched than digging into other people's minds; tend your own inner spirit, and see others with affection. Today's word.
Your line: not my business. Skip one bit of prying today: one profile, one rumor, one question that isn't yours to ask. Day five hundred thirty-seven.

howItsDone: Readers who take this entry to heart often cut back on gossip and checking up on others, and turn that attention to their own character instead.

fork.setup: you notice two coworkers acting strangely, and you could piece together what's going on. what does Meditations 2.13 suggest?
options: let it be, tend your own mind, and treat them kindly.
fork.reveal: it's enough to attend to the spirit within, Marcus says, and to see others with affection, not to pry.

original.note: Greek: a guiding spirit. Marcus's word for the divine part within each person, to be tended and revered.

trapdoor: what you thought: don't be nosy.
what it means: prying is a restless misery; tend the spirit within you, and look on others with affection.
what a scholar hears: Pindar's 'beneath the earth', quoted in Plato's Theaetetus for the roaming philosophic mind, becomes Marcus's picture of the busybody.

notes: Meditations 2.13 paraphrased: nothing more wretched than one who traverses everything in a round and pries into the things beneath the earth, as the poet says, and seeks by conjecture what is in his neighbors' minds; enough to attend to the daemon within and reverence it sincerely, keeping it pure from passion, thoughtlessness and dissatisfaction with gods and men; men deserve affection for kinship, sometimes pity for ignorance of good and bad, a blindness no less than not distinguishing white and black.
